newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe hospitals close as junior doctors strike.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe hospitals close as junior doctors strike.

text.p: Zimbabwe's two main hospitals closed their doors to patients on Wednesday after junior doctors and some other medical staff went on strike to protest against the arrest of two of their colleagues.

"We are turning away all new cases now because there is nobody here to care for patients and all critically ill patients will be discharged," Callistus Madziwa, medical superintendent at Parirenyatwa Hospital, told reporters.
He said the hospital was asking relatives to pick up critically ill patients and care for them at home.
At Harare hospital, the capital's largest, authorities were unavailable for comment but one of the hospital's senior doctors who refused to be named said the situation was "chaotic".
"Harare hospital is also closed to new patients," he told Reuters, adding army medical personnel who have been helping senior doctors handle emergencies were failing to cope.
"The whole health system is in shambles. People are dying, there's no two ways about it," he said.
Surgeons were refering emergency cases to private clinics.
Junior doctors, theatre staff and physiotherapists walked out on Tuesday in protest against the arrest of two leaders of the state Hospitals Doctors Association.

Police arrested the doctors, Farai Jiah and Austin Bene, on Monday and Tuesday on charges of inciting nurses to go on strike on October 21 to press demands for higher pay, allowances and negotiations on their working conditions.
The government reacted to the nurses' strike by firing them -- estimated by union officials to number 10,000 -- last week.
The junior doctors, who had gone on strike together with the nurses last month, returned to their posts a week ago.
Jiah and Bene appeared in a Harare magistrate court on Wednesday for an initial remand hearing.
Their lawyer Tendai Biti applied for their release and told a courtroom packed with striking doctors and nurses that the law under which they were charged violated Zimbabwe's constitution.
"If a worker (in an essential service) commits a misdemeanour, isn't the (labour relations) law enough to deal with it wihtout employing such excessive, fascist provisions?" he asked.
The court is expected to rule on the application for release on Thursday.
